routes.description: Establish that the defended doctrine concerns freely maintained separation and sin's internal consequences, while divine grace, corrective sanctification, and possible annihilation prevent hell from being externally imposed endless torture.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if culpable persistence after adequate disclosure can ground exile, suffering functions as a consequence or restorative process rather than arbitrary torture, rescue remains genuinely available, and final destruction limits otherwise endless suffering.

motionBridge.description: Show that self-chosen exile, sanctifying grace, and possible annihilation jointly provide a morally coherent Christian account of hell distinct from external torture.

centralBridges.description: Establish that informed attachment to pride or self-rule can constitute a responsible refusal of reconciliation rather than mere involuntary disbelief.
Explain infernal suffering as internally developing corruption or painful restoration, with grace available to any soul that genuinely seeks reconciliation.
Account for duration and proportionality by allowing release through transformation, universal reconciliation, or the eventual dissolution of a persistently alienated finite soul.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require adequate information and a fair opportunity for correction so honest confusion is distinguished from persistent informed rejection.
Connect death, exile, final justice, and Christ-mediated rescue to the broader theological framework that gives the proposed alternatives their moral function.

routes.description: Establish that apparent rejection of God is shaped by involuntary belief, misleading information, psychological incapacity, and arbitrary circumstances, so suffering or destruction cannot be justified by calling the resulting separation self-chosen.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the required refusal is not adequately informed and voluntary, if grace and full disclosure instead imply eventual reconciliation, or if the duration, suffering, annihilation, and rescue framework remains disproportionate or internally incoherent.

motionBridge.description: Show that relabeling hell as exile, sanctification, or annihilation does not morally justify its suffering or finality without informed agency, proportionality, and coherent rescue conditions.

centralBridges.description: Establish that belief and apparent rejection arise from evidence, upbringing, psychology, or hiddenness rather than a freely selected preference for separation.
Show that occupants either cannot escape, misunderstand their options, or would seek available grace once informed, undermining continued exile as a voluntary condition.
Test whether finite wrongdoing can justify prolonged suffering or annihilation and whether the theological account of death, exile, and substitution consistently bears that burden.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require a fair opportunity for postmortem clarification and change rather than allowing death or contingent religious circumstances to fix a person's fate.
Determine whether complete information, divine mercy, and universally available grace leave any coherent basis for permanent non-reconciliation.

sections.title: Self-Chosen Exile and Internal Consequences
sections.rationale: This issue defines the proposed alternative to external torture and tests whether pride, self-rule, and progressive moral corruption can make separation and its suffering genuinely attributable to the person.

sections.title: Epistemic Agency, Hiddenness, and Fair Opportunity
sections.rationale: The moral status of exile depends on whether rejection can remain responsible despite involuntary belief formation, motivated reasoning, misinformation, divine hiddenness, and the contingency of death.

sections.title: Sanctifying Grace, Escape, and Universalism
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether painful transformation and available divine assistance make hell escapable, whether incapacity or defective preference defeats voluntariness, and whether the stated rescue conditions imply universal reconciliation.

sections.title: Duration, Proportionality, and Possible Annihilation
sections.rationale: The justification must address the relation between finite wrongdoing and potentially prolonged suffering while determining whether eventual dissolution, continued sin, or release supplies a proportionate final outcome.

sections.title: Final Justice, Death, Exile, and Atonement
sections.rationale: The broader account of divine justice and Christ-mediated rescue bears on what consequence sin incurs, how death or exile is overcome, and whether the proposed hell model fits its theological mechanism of reconciliation.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: Hell is a freely chosen identity grounded apart from God, with suffering arising from continued sin and separation rather than externally imposed divine torture.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex introduces Michael by name, asks him for his account of hell, and Michael's uninterrupted answer follows directly.

response.rationale: Constructive move defining the defended account as voluntary separation with internally generated consequences; no earlier opposing target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: As a constructive, it clearly establishes the central mechanism and its contrast with external torture.

precisionFindings.rationale: The internal-consequence thesis is recoverable, though the conditions making the identity freely chosen remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical description outruns the excerpt's support for voluntariness, although it functions as a proposed model.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from continued sin to freely chosen identity is intelligible but leaves the agency bridge underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt supplies an articulated account but little independent support for freedom, persistence, or causation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable voluntary-separation bridge and defines the proposed alternative.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily states its own model and does not materially interpret a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly contrasts internal consequences of continued sin and separation with external divine torment.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: Escape from hell may remain possible, but sanctification is painful, and souls may remain because surrendering the pride and sinful identity they protect is deeply difficult.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn begins with Michael answering Alex's taxonomy question and continues in his distinctive first-person exposition without interruption.

response.rationale: Constructive move explaining why an available exit might be refused: surrendering pride, identity, and sin is portrayed as painfully difficult.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It develops a central escape-and-sanctification mechanism, though chiefly through a literary illustration.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move explicitly presents possibility and difficulty, but its generalization from depicted souls remains only partly scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Modal language appropriately limits the claim to a possible model of painful sanctification and refusal.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Painful identity change can coherently explain refusal despite escape, with one implicit bridge from difficulty to persistence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Great Divorce example illustrates the model but does not establish how actual souls would choose or change.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central account of restorative suffering and the continued availability of escape.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops its own account without relying on a substantive characterization of an opposing position.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes souls returning from heaven because shedding pride, sin, and identity would be extremely painful.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Potentially endless suffering is disproportionate to finite wrongdoing, so the duration of hell remains morally unjustified even when hell is described as self-chosen rather than externally imposed.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex resumes after restating the four doctrines and develops the skeptical objections in a continuous first-person turn.

response.rationale: Constructive proportionality objection arguing that potentially endless punishment cannot be justified by necessarily finite wrongdoing.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It crisply establishes a central proportionality challenge that the defended duration account must answer.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is expressly conditional on punishment being potentially eternal and clearly identifies finite wrongdoing as its comparator.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker frames the result as a moral problem and expressly limits it to potentially endless punishment.

charity.alternative: Hell may be self-chosen and internally sustained rather than externally imposed punishment.
charity.decisiveQualification: Self-choice alone does not answer whether potentially endless suffering is proportionate to finite wrongdoing.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proportionality inference is clear, though it assumes duration must track the temporal finitude of wrongdoing.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument is principally normative and well stated, but the governing proportionality principle is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central proportionality test for duration and potentially endless suffering.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection expressly grants the softer model and isolates the remaining duration problem fairly.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly contrasts a potentially eternal punishment with what can only be a finite crime.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: Hell may culminate in annihilation rather than endless suffering, while honest error can be healed and culpability instead concerns informed, prideful preference for self-rule.
moves.attributionBasis: Michael explicitly takes up Alex's first objection, states his own annihilationist view, and then answers the deservingness challenge.

components.text: Potentially endless suffering is disproportionate to finite wrongdoing.
Calling hell self-chosen does not itself justify its duration.

response.rationale: Annihilation directly limits endless suffering, while the distinction between honest error and informed rejection addresses who may culpably remain.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move directly contacts the duration premise and offers a finite-outcome alternative, though its support remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: Annihilation and healing of honest rejection are explicit, but their precise timing and culpability threshold remain underdefined.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is appropriately presented as an annihilationist possibility rather than a demonstrated necessary outcome.

charity.alternative: Even self-chosen hell could remain endless and disproportionate.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply avoids endless suffering only if eventual annihilation actually applies to persistent alienation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Annihilation coherently blocks infinite duration, but honest error and prideful rejection require further decision criteria.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt offers theological authorities and distinctions, yet does not independently defend annihilation or culpability conditions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central finite-outcome bridge by replacing endless suffering with possible dissolution.

representationalCharity.rationale: It fairly recognizes the duration concern and answers with a bounded alternative, while leaving implementation underspecified.

moves.evidenceBasis: The move expressly introduces annihilation and quotes the healing of honest rejection while reserving culpability for continued rejection.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Even emphatic anti-theism can reflect a sincere but mistaken pursuit of liberty, and because people do not choose which experiences and arguments convince them, the resulting separation is not fairly self-chosen.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex addresses Michael by name, uses his own former agreement with Hitchens as a personal example, and sustains the full objection.

components.text: Separation and its identity are freely chosen rather than imposed.
Only informed prideful rejection, rather than honest error, is culpable.

response.rationale: The reply contests the decisive voluntariness premise by arguing that sincere conviction follows experience and argument rather than direct choice.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly attacks the agency premise with concrete cases and applies that defect to allegedly self-chosen exile.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between involuntary conviction and chosen separation is clear and applied to specified sincere cases.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is framed as a strong challenge rather than certainty and is supported by a concrete conviction-based account.

charity.alternative: A person may sincerely believe atheism while still cultivating a preference for self-rule.
charity.decisiveQualification: The defense still needs to show that this preference, rather than involuntary conviction, explains the relevant separation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If conviction is not directly chosen, inferring chosen exile from disbelief is invalid without an additional preference bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Personal and Hitchens examples are illustrative rather than representative, but they substantiate the conceptual possibility well.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable con bridge that apparent rejection can arise involuntarily.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants the defended non-eternal variant and targets its strongest remaining agency requirement.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts allegedly chosen separation with experiences and arguments that convinced sincere anti-theists without their choosing conviction.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: Belief is not wholly passive because motivated reasoning can favor arguments supporting desired identities, while reflective agents can recognize these influences and bear responsibility for resisting them.
moves.attributionBasis: Michael announces a pushback against Alex's claim about conviction, cites studies, and applies their implications to himself and other agents.

components.text: People do not choose which experiences and arguments convince them.
Involuntary conviction makes resulting separation morally nonvoluntary.

response.rationale: The reply contacts passivity by adducing motivated selection of congenial arguments, but only partly establishes morally responsible control over subconscious processes.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive agency component, yet the bridge from motivated bias to culpable control remains incomplete.

precisionFindings.rationale: Motivated evaluation is clear, but the scope of awareness and the transition to responsibility are only partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The studies support motivated selection, but the stronger conclusion about moral agency needs an additional control premise.

charity.alternative: Conviction may be influenced by desires while remaining involuntary in the morally relevant sense.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bias establishes causal influence, not necessarily awareness, control, or culpable resistance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Motivated reasoning weakens pure passivity, but subconscious selection does not by itself entail responsible control.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Empirical studies support motivated evaluation, while their application to damnation-level responsibility is materially compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central involuntary-rejection bridge through a competing account of belief formation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes passive belief but insufficiently preserves the opponent's decisive distinction between influence and agency.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites motivated-evaluation research and describes subconscious selection of arguments aligned with prior desires.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Subconscious bias does not restore morally relevant agency, and if Christianity is true, rejection can still result from misleading information or involuntary persuasion rather than culpable refusal.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex explicitly focuses on Michael's use of the word subconsciously and develops a sustained first-person counterexample and conclusion.

components.text: Motivated reasoning supplies morally relevant agency over belief.
Proper information separates honest error from culpable rejection.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the missing inference: subconscious bias may explain conviction without supplying awareness or morally relevant control, preserving unfairness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly identifies why the motivated-reasoning premise fails to establish the required moral consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes causal bias from morally relevant agency and states the informational alternative.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is appropriately framed as an unfairness objection contingent on subconscious or misleading causes.

charity.alternative: Motivated reasoning can sometimes be recognized and deliberately resisted.
charity.decisiveQualification: The cited subconscious cases do not establish that awareness or resistance was available to the condemned individual.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between causal influence and responsible control directly defeats the preceding inference unless further agency is shown.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is strong and grounded in the opponent's subconscious premise, though broader psychology remains undocumented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central involuntary-rejection bridge by denying that bias restores culpable agency.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response allows that informed rejection could differ while preserving the strongest objection concerning subconscious cases.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt emphasizes subconscious influence and misleading information, then denies that either provides morally relevant agency.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: People can become aware of subconscious biases and correct them, while perfect divine justice protects those deprived of truth and adequate evidence need not overcome identity-driven resistance.
moves.attributionBasis: Michael agrees with part of Alex's premise, then answers it through conscious correction, divine justice, and the extended flat-earth analogy.

components.text: Subconscious bias does not provide morally relevant awareness or control.
Sincere mistaken conviction makes exile involuntary.
Misleading information should excuse apparent rejection.

response.rationale: The reply supplies reflective correction and perfect justice as answers, but the flat-earth analogy only partially supports their availability in religious hiddenness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both correction and informational fairness, while leaving their operation and adequacy partly asserted.

precisionFindings.rationale: Correction and divine fairness are explicit, but who can correct bias and what counts as proper information remain underspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker expressly avoids claiming that adequate information necessarily convinces and presents a plausible countermodel.

charity.alternative: Some nonbelief persists because available information is genuinely inadequate rather than identity-protective.
charity.decisiveQualification: Perfect justice is asserted to protect such people, but its practical criteria are not supplied.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Reflective correction can restore agency in some cases, but its availability cannot be inferred from isolated resistant groups.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Scriptural references and the flat-earth analogy provide illustration, not representative support for correction or perfect classification.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central involuntary-rejection bridge by proposing correction and fair excuse conditions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly concedes informational deprivation, though it relies on divine justice rather than fully explaining the classification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes awareness of bias, perfect justice for informational deprivation, and resistant flat-earthers as a counterexample.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: An apparent refusal of heaven cannot be treated as informed self-exile when divine hiddenness and misleading information produce a distorted view of God that God could correct.
moves.attributionBasis: The extended father-and-child analogy is delivered in O'Connor's skeptical first-person voice immediately after Jones's self-chosen-exile account.

components.text: An apparent preference for separation is a freely chosen identity.
Adequate information need not overcome identity-driven resistance.

response.rationale: The analogy argues that apparent refusal rests on a distorted picture which an omnipotent God could correct, directly challenging informed self-exile.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the informed-choice premise and assigns the informational failure to the capable revealer.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly limits its conclusion to refusals based on confusion or misleading information under divine hiddenness.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The analogy is offered as importantly similar rather than identical, with its parody limitation expressly acknowledged.

charity.alternative: Some agents may receive adequate disclosure yet protect an identity opposed to God.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection concerns cases where the apparent refusal is demonstrably based on confusion God could remedy.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If refusal depends on correctable distortion, classifying it as informed self-exile requires a missing justification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The parent-child analogy effectively exposes the principle, though its fit with divine disclosure is not independently established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central involuntary-rejection bridge by linking hiddenness to distorted apparent refusal.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response preserves the possibility of culpable refusal while sharply testing whether the described cases meet that standard.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that ostensible refusal of heaven must rest on confusion and stresses God's ability to correct it.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: If death fixes a person's destination without a fair postmortem opportunity for clarification and change, the result is arbitrary because belief, religious circumstances, and the timing of death are outside individual control.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor resumes the analogy in a sustained skeptical turn, contrasting a potentially persuasive divine encounter with the apparent finality imposed at death.

components.text: Perfect justice protects those deprived of truth and adequate information.
Honest rejection will be forgiven and healed.

response.rationale: The move asks why clarification and evidence are unavailable after death, challenging whether the asserted fairness conditions are actually supplied.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly tests the temporal opportunity implicit in the fairness claim, though the precise defended cutoff is not quoted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The postmortem-opportunity demand is clear, but whether death invariably fixes destination is treated as an assumed condition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The arbitrary-cutoff conclusion is appropriately conditional on death fixing destiny without subsequent clarification.

charity.alternative: Divine justice may excuse honest error without requiring a postmortem evidential encounter.
charity.decisiveQualification: The defense must still explain how fair classification occurs when decisive clarification is withheld before an uncontrolled death.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If fate is fixed at an uncontrolled cutoff before available clarification, arbitrariness follows absent a relevant death-based distinction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument is conceptually supported, but the asserted universal finality at death is not fully documented in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the subsidiary demand for fair postmortem clarification and opportunity to change.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly focuses on opportunity rather than assuming that mere disbelief automatically deserves rescue.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt imagines God answering objections and providing existence evidence, highlighting the missing opportunity if death forecloses it.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: Biblical images of Gehenna can describe progressive moral degradation in which unchecked sin becomes internally consuming, destroys the person, and may cause harm to others.
moves.attributionBasis: Jones answers the ontology question through a continuous exposition of Gehenna, prophetic imagery, and the rich-man narrative.

components.text: Hiddenness and misinformation make apparent refusal uninformed rather than self-chosen.
Involuntary conviction prevents fair attribution of separation.

response.rationale: Progressive internal corruption bears on hell's ontology and consequences but does not answer whether initial or continuing refusal is adequately informed.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is relevant contrary material about internal consequences, yet leaves the decisive hiddenness and agency demand uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The degradation mechanism is recoverable, but its universality, pace, and relationship to voluntary choice remain partly scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move uses possibility language for outward harm, but states the internal degradation trajectory more strongly than supported.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Unchecked wrongdoing can coherently compound, but the leap to soul-destroying infernal progression needs a bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Biblical imagery and moral illustration support intelligibility, not the asserted postmortem causal process.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central internal-suffering bridge by describing suffering as developing corruption.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily develops an internal-corruption model rather than interpreting the hiddenness objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes unchecked sin becoming a consuming internal fire that degrades the person and may harm others.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: Endless existence in hell is unnecessary because finite souls moving continually away from God may disintegrate, while a soul that turns toward God can leave through painful restoration.
moves.attributionBasis: Jones directly answers the question about eternal punishment, distinguishes his view from an immortality defense, and states his own annihilation-and-escape position.

components.text: Potentially endless suffering is disproportionate to finite wrongdoing.
A fair opportunity for clarification and change should remain available.

response.rationale: The move directly denies necessary endlessness through eventual dissolution and also permits departure through painful restoration after turning toward God.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers duration with a finite terminus and preserves an escape route, while the dissolution inference remains underdefended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two outcomes are explicit, but the timing and metaphysical rule linking finitude to disintegration are underspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker calls disintegration a logical consequence, a stronger claim than the supplied premises establish.

charity.alternative: A finite soul might be divinely sustained indefinitely despite continued alienation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Finitude alone does not logically entail eventual nonexistence without an added dependence or decay premise.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Finite status plus movement away from God does not alone entail dissolution, though the proposed outcome is internally possible.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The metaphysical conclusion is asserted with limited support, and named authorities do not establish the needed causal warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable finite-outcome bridge through dissolution or restorative release.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply acknowledges an immortality defense but understates the additional premise needed to defeat it.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that finite souls moving continually away from God eventually disintegrate and that turning souls may leave.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The addiction analogy undermines wholly self-chosen hell because occupants either recognize the better alternative but lack the ability to escape, or prefer remaining only because they misunderstand that alternative.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor develops a sustained two-case analysis of addiction and applies both alternatives explicitly to the asserted choice between heaven and hell.

components.text: Souls may remain because surrendering sinful identity is painfully difficult.
Continued separation is wholly self-chosen.
A soul can leave by turning toward God through painful restoration.

response.rationale: The two-case dilemma identifies why difficulty does not establish free preference: occupants either lack ability or misunderstand which alternative is better.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly diagnoses the decisive defect and states the consequence for both voluntariness and escape.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alternatives are distinctly stated and their implications for ability, information, and preference are explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the stipulated goodness of heaven, the exhaustive ability-or-information dilemma is proportionately asserted.

charity.alternative: An informed person may possess capacity yet still prefer sin because transformation is painfully costly.
charity.decisiveQualification: If the person recognizes the better outcome and can obtain it, the defense must explain why refusal is more than impaired preference.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dilemma is forceful under the stipulated goodness of heaven, though mixed cases of partial ability remain possible.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The addiction analogy robustly supports the conceptual distinction, with one bounded gap concerning its exact infernal fit.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly establishes the central escape dilemma concerning incapacity, misinformation, and voluntariness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response engages the strongest painful-choice account and isolates the unresolved capacity or valuation defect.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly divides occupants into those recognizing the better option but lacking ability and those misunderstanding the option.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: A soul unable to escape hell through its own strength need only seek Christ's grace, which remains available to carry it through sanctification and into reconciliation.
moves.attributionBasis: Jones responds immediately to the addiction dilemma by invoking grace, rehabilitation assistance, Christ's saving action, and forgiveness beyond the core boundary.

components.text: An occupant recognizing the better alternative may lack strength or ability to escape.
An occupant may remain because the better alternative is misunderstood.

response.rationale: Grace directly answers the incapacity branch by supplying external assistance, but it does not answer the misinformation branch or why all sufferers would not ask.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive incapacity component but leaves the second branch of the dilemma unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The condition of asking for grace and the claimed result of assistance through sanctification are expressly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Saying the answer is simply to ask understates possible inability to seek, misinformation, or defective preference.

charity.alternative: Addicted agents may lack not only execution strength but also the capacity to form or sustain the request for help.
charity.decisiveQualification: Grace answers inability only if a genuine request remains psychologically and epistemically available.

logicalCoherence.rationale: External grace can solve insufficient strength, but the solution assumes the very help-seeking capacity placed in question.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The theological mechanism is clearly asserted yet receives little support for universal availability or effective uptake.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central escape dilemma by offering grace as assistance beyond personal strength.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response takes incapacity seriously but compresses the opponent's strongest concern into a readily performable request.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says Christ carries and sanctifies sufferers and that one wishing to escape need only ask for grace and forgiveness.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Universally available grace appears to entail universalism because informed sufferers would request forgiveness, while sufferers who remain misinformed would merit mercy rather than continued damnation.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly draws a philosophical implication from Jones's preceding concessions and develops both branches of the dilemma.

components.text: Any suffering soul can obtain rescue simply by requesting grace and forgiveness.
Genuine misinformation merits forgiveness and healing.
Some souls may remain despite escape being available.

response.rationale: The reply combines informed request and excusable misinformation into a dilemma under which neither branch coherently leaves a soul permanently unreconciled.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the consequence of the prior concessions and covers both informed and misinformed occupants.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two branches and the resulting universalist pressure are clearly and conditionally articulated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents universalism as an apparent implication and states the precise concessions generating it.

charity.alternative: An informed occupant might knowingly refuse available grace despite suffering.
charity.decisiveQualification: The defense must explain why anyone who understands both options would neither request rescue nor merit mercy.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Given universally effective requested grace and mercy for genuine misinformation, the universalist pressure follows strongly.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument relies closely on the opponent's concessions, though the empirical premise that every informed sufferer asks remains undefended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary universalism-pressure bridge and nearly supplies its full inferential demand.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply considers both information states and isolates the strongest remaining possibility of informed refusal.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that informed sufferers request forgiveness while genuinely misinformed sufferers independently deserve mercy.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: If unrepentant humans incur hell or separation from God, genuine substitutionary payment requires Jesus to undergo that same consequence rather than merely enter hell without suffering humanity's penalty.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor develops a sustained first-person objection to the adequacy of Jesus's sacrifice and repeatedly frames the required consequence.

components.text: Christ's grace carries sinners through sanctification and reconciliation.
Hell or final destruction is the consequence incurred by persistent rejection.

response.rationale: The move raises a coherent substitution challenge to the broader rescue framework but does not contact the immediate mechanism by which grace enables escape.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a secondary consequence premise while leaving the decisive grace-and-escape component unaddressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The required equivalence between the sinner's consequence and the substitute's experience is clearly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Within genuine penal substitution, requiring the substitute to bear the relevant penalty is proportionately stated.

charity.alternative: Atonement may work through representative victory or reconciliation rather than strict identical punishment.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection applies conditionally where the defense describes Jesus as paying the price humans otherwise bear.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If substitution means payment of the same liability, failure to bear that consequence creates a clear inconsistency.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The inference is conceptually strong, though the defense's commitment to strict identity of penalty is not fully documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central proportionality-and-coherence bridge through the atonement mechanism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move appropriately targets payment language but only implicitly limits its conclusion to a strict substitutionary model.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks whether Jesus experienced separation because otherwise he would not pay the consequence assigned to sinners.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: The biblical consequence of sin is death and exile, which Jesus bears through his death and experienced separation from the Father on the cross.
moves.attributionBasis: Jones directly answers by defining sin's consequence and applying death, exile, and divine separation to the crucifixion narrative.

components.text: A genuine substitute must undergo the same relevant consequence incurred by sinners.
Jesus merely entered hell without suffering humanity's penalty.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the penalty as death and exile, then claims Jesus bore both through death and experienced separation on the cross.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the demanded equivalence by specifying the consequence and matching Christ's experience to it.

precisionFindings.rationale: Death and exile are clear categories, but separation shifts between temporal experience and eternal separation language.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The scriptural interpretation is asserted categorically despite ambiguity about forsakenness and the nature of divine separation.

charity.alternative: The human penalty includes prolonged or final separation beyond ordinary death.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must show that the cross's death and forsakenness instantiate that same consequence rather than symbolize it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The matching inference works if death and exile exhaust the penalty, but that characterization is the disputed premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Scriptural phrases support death and forsakenness, while the claimed eternal divine separation remains underdefended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central coherence objection by specifying how the cross bears death and exile.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response squarely addresses identical consequence, but compresses the opponent's duration and identity concerns.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines sin's consequence as death and exile and applies crucifixion and forsakenness to Jesus.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The death described as sin's wages may need to mean spiritual annihilation rather than ordinary physical death, because physical death occurs to everyone and cannot distinguish the asserted final penalty.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor poses a focused conceptual challenge immediately after Jones distinguishes death from hell as the scriptural penalty.

components.text: The relevant consequence of sin is death and exile, which Jesus bears.
Persistent alienation may terminate in spiritual dissolution.

response.rationale: The focused question challenges equivocation over death by noting that universal physical death cannot distinguish the asserted final penalty.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the definition of the consequence and identifies the need for a spiritually discriminating sense.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes ordinary physical death from possible spiritual annihilation and frames the latter tentatively.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The challenge is properly interrogative and uses tentative language for spiritual annihilation rather than asserting it.

charity.alternative: Physical death can be a universal consequence of sin even if it does not distinguish final destinies.
charity.decisiveQualification: The defense still must explain how universal death constitutes the special liability allegedly substituted for.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Universal physical death creates a real explanatory problem, but does not logically preclude its being sin's consequence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The universal occurrence of physical death supports the conceptual challenge without requiring extensive external evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central coherence test concerning the identity of sin's penalty and annihilation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The question fairly probes the meaning of death, though distinguishability is not strictly required by every account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks which death is meant and contrasts universal physical death with spiritual annihilation.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: A temporary crucifixion followed by resurrection and eternal exaltation appears disproportionately small compared with humanity's cumulative sins and the death or separation said to be their deserved consequence.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly formulates an objection about whether Jesus pays an adequate price and contrasts crucifixion with humanity's alleged liability.

components.text: Jesus bears humanity's consequence through death and separation on the cross.
Crucifixion and forsakenness adequately match humanity's cumulative liability.

response.rationale: The reply directly compares the finite crucifixion followed by exaltation with humanity's cumulative alleged liability and questions proportional adequacy.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly contacts the adequacy of the proposed payment through an explicit magnitude and duration comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The temporal and magnitude comparison is clear, and the conclusion is explicitly framed as an appearance of disproportion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents an apparent proportionality problem rather than claiming a mathematically proven imbalance.

charity.alternative: The divine identity of the sufferer could give finite-duration suffering extraordinary value.
charity.decisiveQualification: Identity alone needs a defended metric connecting divine suffering to the aggregate liability it allegedly pays.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The disparity creates a strong prima facie challenge, though duration alone need not determine atonement's value.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The contrast is grounded in the described events, but the proportionality metric remains materially implicit.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central proportionality-and-coherence bridge by testing the asserted payment's adequacy.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection leaves room for special significance while requiring an account of how that significance establishes adequacy.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts crucifixion and rapid resurrection to exaltation with humanity's depravity, death, and separation liability.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.proposition: The crucifixion has immeasurable weight because the divine Son experiences rupture within the Trinity's perfect unity, making its significance greater than its finite duration suggests.
moves.attributionBasis: Jones directly answers the proportionality objection by invoking Christ's full divinity, trinitarian unity, and the magnitude of divine anguish.

components.text: A temporary crucifixion appears too small to pay humanity's cumulative liability.
The substitute must genuinely experience the relevant separation.

response.rationale: The reply answers temporal disproportion by locating immeasurable weight in divine trinitarian rupture, although it does not supply a metric connecting infinity to payment.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the magnitude objection with a relevant identity-based account, but leaves a central warrant compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed divine rupture is recoverable, but separation within perfect unity and infinite weight remain metaphysically unstable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling the event beyond torment because it involves an infinite being exceeds the argument supplied for magnitude or equivalence.

charity.alternative: Finite-duration suffering can have extraordinary significance without equaling every sinner's alleged penalty.
charity.decisiveQualification: The defense must establish why divine identity yields sufficient penal equivalence rather than merely unique anguish.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Divine identity could affect significance, but infinity of being does not by itself entail infinite suffering or adequate payment.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The trinitarian premises and magnitude inference are largely asserted, with no defended measure of rupture or substitution.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central atonement proportionality objection by addressing magnitude rather than duration alone.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response recognizes the strongest proportionality challenge but partially substitutes asserted infinity for the required equivalence warrant.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that rupture within divine perfect unity is beyond finite torment because it happens to an infinite being.
